title: Congestion pricing can make emergency medical response faster inside a city pricing zone
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35414, using New York City congestion-zone boundary, traffic and mobility measures, and emergency medical service performance
geography: New York City; congestion-relief zone boundary at 60th Street

observations.period: January 5, 2025 congestion-pricing implementation and early post-implementation period

denominator.unit: Traffic observations, mobility measures, and EMS events used in the study; public abstract does not state exact counts

vehicle_traffic.value: declined by roughly 18% to 21% near the zone boundary

ems_total_travel_time.value: decreased by 63 to 70 seconds, approximately 5% to 6%
ems_total_travel_time.unit: reported change in total EMS travel time

spillover.value: little evidence of displacement to adjacent areas

patient_outcomes.value: not observed in the public abstract
patient_outcomes.unit: missing survival, treatment, cost, and distributional patient outcomes

observations.method: Difference-in-discontinuities design exploiting the sharp geographic boundary of New York City's congestion-relief zone; the paper separates the traffic first stage from EMS performance and notes that a concurrent FDNY nearest-hospital directive confounds standard difference-in-differences estimates.
observations.uncertainty: The public abstract does not disclose the full event counts, exact study window, subgroup estimates, or all robustness results. The measured response-time improvement does not by itself show improved survival, equal benefit across neighborhoods, or that the policy's total costs were socially acceptable.
observations.subgroup: EMS events and traffic/mobility observations inside and near the congestion-pricing boundary; individual patients, household income, ability to avoid the charge, and neighborhood-level distribution of benefits and burdens are not linked.
observations.counterinterpretation: The result may be specific to a dense Manhattan boundary and the early implementation period. Changes in emergency routing, hospital destination, traffic composition, pedestrian and bicycle activity, or enforcement could affect measured outcomes; faster travel is not the same as better care or lower household burden.

related_sources.claim: NBER's public summary describes the boundary design and the approximately one-minute EMS travel-time improvement.

boundary: This record adds a measured policy-to-service route: congestion pricing changed traffic conditions and EMS travel time near a New York City boundary. It does not establish patient survival, treatment quality, affordability, distributional fairness, long-run traffic adaptation, or political acceptance of the charge.
